As I read aloud, listen for what Percy values and what he fears."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about 90 seconds of partner talk and one or two shares. Say: 'The root *mort-* comes from Latin and means death. Let's use it to work out a word you will meet on page 6 of The Lightning Thief.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"If *mort-* means death, what does *mortal* mean? The prefix *im-* means 'not.' So what does *immortal* mean?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Mortal means someone who can die. Immortal must mean not able to die, so someone who lives forever, like the Greek gods."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Great. Now let's verify that guess: we'll check it against the sentence on page 6 when we read, and against the glossary or a dictionary. Verifying is how we make sure our thinking is right."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Next word part: *-ology* means 'the study of.' Think of *biology*, the study of life. What does *mythology* mean?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Mythology is the study of myths, or all the myths of a culture put together, like Greek mythology."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Last word part: *trans-* means 'across' or 'change.' What might *transport* mean? What about *transform*?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Transport is to carry something across from one place to another. Transform is to change something all the way into something else, like a caterpillar into a butterfly."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Notice these parts show up in myth language all the time. Gods transform into animals, mortals are carried across the sea, and the stories are called mythology. Keep these parts in your pocket as we read the rest of the unit."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"This is a quick word-building routine, not a context-clues review. Keep the pace brisk: about 2 minutes per word part. Part C: Students use evidence to predict whether Percy is set up as a hero or a 'problem' figure, and state an emerging theme.","activities":[{"id":"lia-read-aloud-think-aloud","title":"Part A: Listen and Collect Evidence (Read-Aloud with Think-Alouds)","minutes":12,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","L.6.4","L.6.4.a","L.6.4.d","RL.6.10"],"routine":"Teacher Read-Aloud and Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"directions","text":"Follow along in your book as I read pages 1–8 aloud. Use a two-column chart: in the left column write 'What Percy says or does (quote)' and in the right column write 'What this shows he values or fears.' Add two or three entries as we pause."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Read with energy and pace: pause for effect, slow down when Percy speaks directly to the reader, and speed up when the narration turns sarcastic. Stop for think-alouds only at the points below (about 4 pauses). Use your copy's exact wording when you quote."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Pause 1, after Percy's opening warning on page 1 ('Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood...'). Think aloud: 'Percy starts by telling me to stop reading. That's strange for a book narrator. He says being a half-blood is dangerous and scary. And he says he *envies* readers who think it's just fiction. *Envy* means wishing you had what someone else has. So he wishes he could believe none of this was real, which tells me he'd rather be a regular kid. I'll write that in my chart.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy's warning suggest he values, and what does he fear?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He values a safe, normal life. He fears being a half-blood because he says it's dangerous and 'gets you killed in painful, nasty ways.' He even envies kids who think this is just a made-up story."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Pause 2, at the description of Yancy Academy and Percy's school troubles (pp. 2–3). Think aloud: 'The text says Percy has been *expelled* from schools, and now he's on *probation*. I know *expel* means to force out, and the sentence is about getting kicked out of schools. Probation sounds like a warning period. If I check the sentence, it says one more mistake could cost him, so my guess is right. This shows Percy is used to being seen as a troublemaker.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details about school make Percy seem like the opposite of a 'normal' kid in other people's eyes?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He's been expelled from other schools, he's on probation, and he's at a school for troubled kids. People see him as trouble, even if he says it isn't his fault."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Pause 3, at the field trip and the moment the teacher or classmates *threaten* or punish him, including *detention* (p. 4). Think aloud: 'I notice words like *threatened* and *detention* all clustered together. They are school punishments. The author is stacking them to show how much Percy expects to be blamed. Even before the monster shows up, Percy is worried about being in trouble, which makes me think his fear of being the 'problem kid' is as strong as his fear of monsters.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Pause 4, at the mention of *dyslexia* (p. 7) and the word *immortal* (p. 6). Think aloud: 'Here's the word *immortal*, the one we built earlier. It's about gods who live forever, which contrasts with Percy's very normal worries. And *dyslexia* is a learning difference that makes reading harder. Percy mentions it plainly, so I'll note how he describes himself: not as a hero, but as a kid who has a hard time. That helps me infer what he thinks of himself.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do you infer about Percy from how he talks about himself and school? Use one detail as evidence."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I infer that Percy doesn't think of himself as special or brave. He talks about being kicked out and having dyslexia and ADHD, so he sees himself as a kid who struggles. He wants to be normal, but other people label him as trouble."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Update your definitions for these words in your organizers now: envy, expelled, probation, threatened, detention, immortal, dyslexia. Use your own words and the sentence from the text."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"In the first pages of Chapter 1, why does Percy tell readers to close the book?","choices":[{"text":"He believes being a half-blood is dangerous, and he wants readers to avoid that life.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. Percy says being a half-blood is scary and can get you killed, so he warns readers to stop reading and try to lead a normal life."},{"text":"He thinks his story is boring and wants to save readers' time.","correct":false,"rationale":"Believable but incorrect. His warning is about danger, not boredom. Percy's tone is joking, but his message is serious."},{"text":"He wants to keep his secret from his mom.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. He addresses the reader, and the warning is about the risks of being a half-blood, not hiding something from his mother."},{"text":"He believes only adults should read stories about monsters.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. Percy never says anything about age. He says the story is dangerous for anyone who might be a half-blood."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely and using evidence from Percy's narration to explain what he values and fears.","sayAsk":"Provide a copy of pp. 1–8 with key passages marked. Model: Percy says '___,' which shows he values/fears ___. Prompt students to retell a pause in a short sentence with an adverbial detail, such as 'Percy warns readers at the very start because he fears danger.' Frames: When Percy says ___, I infer ___. This is evidence that ___. Allow home-language rehearsal before sharing in English.","watchFor":"If students retell the plot without inference, then prompt: 'What does that detail show about what Percy wants?' If students copy a quote with no explanation, then prompt: 'Finish: This shows that Percy ___.' Success: students pair a quote with an inference and explain it using a frame."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: making an inference from a quote","tryThis":"Offer a stem: Percy says ___. That makes me think ___ because ___. Use the prompt pair 'What does the text say? What does that tell me about Percy?' with one quote before students work alone."},{"type":"support-table-placeholder-removed","tryThis":""}]}]},{"id":"lia-tone-word-choice","title":"Part B: Tone and Word Choice","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.4","RL.6.6","L.6.4","L.6.5"],"routine":"Annotation and Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1","pages":"pp. 1–4"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the first page. Underline two words or phrases that sound like Percy is talking to you the way a kid talks, informal or sarcastic. Next to each, write the tone it creates (for example: casual, joking, annoyed, honest) and the first impression it gives of Percy."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Tone is the attitude a narrator shows, and it comes from word choice. Compare two ways to say the same thing: 'I would prefer that readers not continue,' versus 'Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood.' The first sounds formal. The second sounds like a kid talking to a friend. Same message, different tone, different first impression."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words or phrases make Percy sound informal or sarcastic? What does that tone make you think about him?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"'Look,' at the start sounds like he's talking to me directly, like he's annoyed or tired. Telling readers to 'close this book right now' sounds blunt and a little sarcastic. It makes him seem honest and funny, but also like someone who's been through a lot."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the funny, casual tone make the scary parts feel different? Why might Riordan have Percy tell the story this way?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The humor makes the story easy to read and makes Percy feel real. But it also shows he's using jokes to cover up being scared. Riordan makes a myth feel modern by giving the hero a voice like a real kid today."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Turn and tell your partner your sentence: 'Percy's word choice, ___, creates a ___ tone, which makes me think he is ___.' Add one detail that tells when, how, or why, like 'right from the first line' or 'because he is warning us.'"},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.6"],"stem":"Which description best explains how Percy's opening word choices shape the tone?","choices":[{"text":"His casual, blunt phrases make him sound like a real kid who is honest and a bit sarcastic about a scary subject.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. Phrases like 'Look' and 'close this book right now' are conversational and blunt, creating an informal, sarcastic tone."},{"text":"His long, formal sentences make him sound like a serious scholar.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. Percy's narration is informal and direct, not formal or scholarly."},{"text":"His excited words show he can't wait to tell readers about being a half-blood.","correct":false,"rationale":"Believable but wrong. He warns readers away and says he did not want to be a half-blood, so he is not excited."},{"text":"His quiet, shy words show he is afraid to talk to readers.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. He speaks to readers directly and boldly, even bossily. His fear shows in what he says, not in shy wording."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in evaluating language choices and expanding sentences with adverbials to explain how word choice creates tone.","sayAsk":"Model: 'At the very start, Percy warns readers bluntly.' Then expand: 'Percy speaks informally to readers because he wants them to trust him.' Frames: The phrase ___ sounds ___ because ___. This creates a ___ tone. In the opening, Percy speaks ___ (how) to ___ (who). Provide a word bank: casual, blunt, sarcastic, honest, joking.","watchFor":"If students say 'he sounds funny' without naming words, then prompt: 'Which exact words? Point to them.' If students write short sentences, then prompt: 'Add when, how, or why to your sentence.' Success: students name a phrase, identify the tone, and expand the sentence with a detail."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: describing tone","tryThis":"Give a tone word bank (casual, joking, blunt, nervous, honest) and have students choose one for each underlined phrase. Ask 'Would a teacher say it this way, or a kid?'"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite Percy's opening line in a formal tone, then explain how the change alters the reader's first impression of him."}]}]},{"id":"lia-hero-or-problem","title":"Part C: Hero or 'Problem'? Predict and Name an Emerging Theme","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.3","RL.6.5"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1","pages":"pp. 1–8"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In myths, heroes are often seen as strangers or troublemakers before they prove themselves. Use your chart to decide how these opening pages might be setting Percy up to be a hero, or a 'problem' figure, in a modern myth. Think about how the opening pages fit into the whole story: what does this chapter set in motion?"},{"type":"directions","text":"Write 3–4 sentences. Start with: 'These opening pages set Percy up as a ___ figure because ___.' Include at least one quote or specific detail from pp. 1–8, and finish with: 'One theme that may be emerging is ___.' Keep your summary of the evidence separate from your opinion about whether you like Percy."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which details from pages 1–8 make Percy look like a 'problem' to people around him, and which suggest he could become a hero?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He looks like a problem because he's been expelled, he's on probation, and teachers expect him to cause trouble. He could be a hero because he's honest, he warns others to stay safe, and he is dealing with huge danger even though he just wants a normal life."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What idea about 'normal' versus 'different' might this story be building toward?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Maybe the theme is that kids who get labeled as problems or not normal may actually have special strengths. Percy wants to be normal, but being different may be what makes him a hero."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Sample paragraph: These opening pages set Percy up as a reluctant hero because he says, 'I didn't want to be a half-blood,' and warns readers about the danger, yet people at school see him as a troublemaker. His sarcastic voice hides how much he fears being different. One theme that may be emerging is that being labeled 'not normal' can hide a person's real strength."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Accept predictions grounded in evidence even if they differ. A strong response uses a quote or detail from pp. 1–8. Collect the paragraphs as a quick formative check for Lesson 5's explanatory writing. Collect organizers to see which vocabulary needs revisiting."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in making evidence-based predictions and writing connected sentences that explain a developing theme.","sayAsk":"Provide frames: These pages set Percy up as ___ because ___. For example, the text says '___.' One theme that may be emerging is ___. Encourage students to add adverbials: 'at the beginning,' 'because of his past,' 'in a quiet way.' Allow oral rehearsal with a partner before writing.","watchFor":"If students predict without evidence, then prompt: 'Which sentence from pages 1–8 made you think that?' If students state only opinions ('he's cool'), then prompt: 'What does the text show, not just how you feel?' Success: students state a prediction, cite a detail, and name a theme in complete sentences."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: connecting evidence to a theme","tryThis":"Give a three-step scaffold: 1) Write one thing Percy says. 2) Write what it shows he values or fears. 3) Write a bigger idea about 'normal' and 'different.' Let students talk each step with a partner first."},{"type":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to compare Percy's opening to a hero from a myth or story they know, and explain what makes Percy a 'modern' hero."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students summarize what Percy's voice shows and reflect on how word parts and evidence helped them today.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-reflection","title":"Exit Reflection","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.2","L.6.4"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In the Performance Task, you will explain a theme and support it with evidence. Today you started that work by noticing what Percy values and fears and how his voice shapes our first impression."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the frames: 'Percy's opening shows he values ___ and fears ___. The word choice ___ creates a ___ tone. The word part ___ helped me figure out the meaning of ___.'"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy's opening shows he values a normal, safe life and fears the danger of being a half-blood and being labeled trouble. The phrase 'Look, I didn't want to be a half-blood' creates a blunt, sarcastic tone. The word part mort- helped me figure out that immortal means living forever."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"If time is short, have students share only the last sentence with a partner. Check organizers for the ten vocabulary words as they leave."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Optional reading and annotation that extends the lesson and connects Percy's story to an older tale.","activities":[{"id":"homework-reading","title":"Read and Annotate","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1 (continued)","pages":"pp. 9–15"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read and annotate The Lightning Thief, Chapter 1, pp. 9–15. Mark one detail that shows what Percy fears and one that shows how people see him."},{"type":"directions","text":"Read and annotate the excerpt from 'The Hare and the Lion.'
